overview.text: The Beatles were an English rock band formed in Liverpool and became a defining act of 1960s popular music. Their best-known lineup—John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison, and Ringo Starr—took shape by 1962. The group became a British sensation in 1963 and helped lead the British Invasion of the United States the following year. Their sound combined rock-and-roll energy with close pop harmonies, while their songwriting and experimentation helped expand what rock music could sound like. They drew on American performers and incorporated styles including ballads, hard rock, and traditional Indian music. The Beatles stopped touring in 1966 and broke up in 1970.

key_facts.text: The band began with three teenage musicians in Liverpool in the late 1950s; Ringo Starr joined after earlier lineup changes, and the Beatles had emerged by 1962.
The group became a national sensation in the United Kingdom in 1963, with a run of number-one singles.
Their first appearance on The Ed Sullivan Show was on February 9, 1964, bringing them to a large U.S. audience.
Their musical roots included American performers such as Buddy Holly, Chuck Berry, and Fats Domino; later recordings also drew on styles such as traditional Indian music and hard rock.
The Rock & Roll Hall of Fame highlights their original songwriting, pop harmonies, rock energy, and willingness to experiment as distinctive parts of their sound.
